chapter: Italy and the future of New Orleans jazz
title: Dixieland's growing popularity in Italy
summary: Reading Italian magazines, he sees a strong trend toward Dixieland there, recalls Louis Armstrong's visit, and hopes to help the new groups.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Okay, we had it all for a second there. Go ahead, Rudy, about going to Italy.

Well, what I wanted to say, or I think would interest you, is that naturally I've been buying a lot of Italian magazines. I've been keeping up with the news in Italy. And I know there is a tremendous trend toward Dixieland music in Italy. They like it. They really love it. In fact, they have a lot of groups coming up. They may not sound like the original Dixieland that we have in America, but at least they're trying. And, boy, I give them credit. Because they like it and they're trying very hard to do it. And I expect I'm going to be doing a lot of playing, and I might even be able to help some of these groups along with what little I learned here in New Orleans. But, well, you know, when Louis Armstrong went to Italy, he got sick in Italy, you know. I got letters back from Italy telling me how glad they were that he was there and that, you know, and how I enjoyed his playing and how... And they asked me very important questions. And I even read an article where somebody was against jazz and they were having some kind of an argument about... Somebody called Shelley Mann a saxophone player.

Well, there you go. So there was a repercussion letter in the bottom saying, how can you talk about jazz against jazz if you don't even know what you're talking about, which was a very good point. So you see, from those arguments, you can see that they like jazz over there and they want it and they're getting it. They want to improve on it and they're going to improve on it. I think it's a wonderful thing.
